page_title: The Infinite Hows (or, the Dangers Of The Five Whys)

sources.entry: The Infinite Hows criticizes the five whys method and advocates for a different set of questions to learn from the most from incidents.

summary.title: The Infinite Hows (or, the Dangers Of The Five Whys)
summary.one_liner: The Five Whys post-mortem technique can lock investigators into oversimplified causal chains and blame individuals, so asking "how?" and seeking second stories yields better learning from incidents.
keywords: sidney dekker field guide to understanding human error
nancy leveson engineering a safer world
takeaways: Asking 'why?' in a chain tends to produce first stories that blame individuals or 'human error' rather than describe systemic conditions.
Asking 'how?' elicits narratives that reveal operational data and the local rationality behind people's decisions.
Root causes are constructed by where investigators start and stop asking questions, not discovered in the rubble.
Use structured prompts (cues, interpretation, goals, time pressure, help) at each critical juncture of an incident, as adapted from Gary Klein and Sidney Dekker.
summary.summary: The author critiques the Five Whys root-cause method, arguing that a chain of "why?" questions assumes too much about causality, ends at individual attributes, and produces "first stories" that can harm learning and safety. The post draws on Dekker, Leveson, Hollnagel, Klein and Carroll, including the ideas of local rationality and "root cause seduction." It proposes replacing "why?" with "how?" questions that gather "second stories," with a four-step approach and a list of debriefing prompts. It ends with links to the author's Velocity tutorials and a longer epilogue on complexity theory.
